set1.io: h — Compare and contrast the pathogenesis of retinal detachment
set1.q: Which primary aetiology does the deck give for TRACTIONAL retinal detachment?
opts: Proliferative diabetic retinopathy
Correct — the neovascular membranes of proliferative disease are the classic traction source.
Severe malignant hypertension
That appears under exudative detachment.
Posterior vitreous detachment
That is a rhegmatogenous risk factor.
Choroidal melanoma
That is an exudative cause.

set1.io: i — Describe the pathologic process of macular degeneration
set1.q: What proportion of severe blindness from macular degeneration does the wet form account for?
opts: About ten per cent
That inverts the deck's figure.
About ninety per cent
Correct — the deck's figure, despite the dry form being commoner.
About fifty per cent
Below the deck's figure.
About twenty-five per cent
Well below the deck's figure.

set1.io: a — Compare and contrast the neurological anatomy of the eye
set1.q: Why does the deck say the outer, easily visible structures are grouped first?
opts: They are the only structures visible without an ophthalmoscope
The deck's grouping is by susceptibility rather than by visibility alone.
They contain the highest density of nerve endings
Not the deck's stated reason.
They are the last to be affected in systemic disease
The deck ties systemic disease to the deepest group.
They are more susceptible to infection, trauma and environmental change
Correct — the deck's reason for the first group.

set1.io: d — Compare and contrast the conditions caused by abnormal shapes of the eye
set1.q: What is amblyopia?
opts: Opacification of the crystalline lens
That is cataract.
Reduced best-corrected visual acuity from abnormal visual processing during the critical developmental period
Correct — the deck's definition, and it is a visual deficit rather than a mechanical one.
Ocular misalignment arising from extraocular muscle imbalance or nerve palsy
That is strabismus, which the deck contrasts with amblyopia.
Progressive optic neuropathy from raised pressure
That is glaucoma.

set1.io: i — Describe the pathologic process of macular degeneration
set1.q: What is the mechanism of wet, neovascular macular degeneration?
opts: Hypoxia and inflammation trigger choroidal neovascularisation, and new vessels breach beneath the pigment epithelium into the subretinal space
Correct — the deck's mechanism, from trigger through to breach.
Extracellular lipofuscin debris accumulating beneath the retinal pigment epithelium
That is the dry form's drusen.
Fibrovascular membranes on the retinal surface exert traction
That is tractional retinal detachment.
Ganglion cell axons undergo apoptosis from raised pressure
That is glaucoma.

set1.io: h — Compare and contrast the pathogenesis of retinal detachment
set1.q: What happens to the vitreous with age, and why does it matter for detachment?
opts: It becomes vascularised, bleeding into the subretinal space
The vitreous stays avascular.
It thickens and opacifies, blocking light before it reaches the retina
That is not the age change the deck or lecture describes.
It liquefies, so fluid can track through any retinal break into the subretinal space
Correct — Webster's jelly-in-the-fridge analogy, and the reason liquefaction is upstream of detachment.
It solidifies, pressing the retina more firmly against the pigment epithelium
The change is towards liquefaction, not solidification.

set1.io: f — Describe the pathogenesis of glaucoma
set1.q: Above what cup-to-disc ratio does the deck describe progressive optic disc cupping?
opts: Greater than 1.0
A ratio above one is not anatomically possible.
Greater than 0.5
Correct — the deck's threshold for an increased cup-to-disc ratio.
Greater than 0.2
Below the deck's stated threshold.
Greater than 0.8
Above the deck's stated threshold.

set1.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
set1.q: Which findings does the deck give for orbital cellulitis that periorbital cellulitis lacks?
opts: Erythema and oedema of the lid alone, held forward by the orbital septum
That is the periorbital picture.
Crusting of the lid margin with altered tear film
That is blepharitis.
A yellowish nodule that does not cross the cornea
That is a pinguecula.
Proptosis, decreased extraocular movement and a risk of optic nerve compression
Correct — the deck's discriminating findings, all consequences of a post-septal collection.

set1.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
set1.q: What is the classical corneal finding in herpes simplex epithelial keratitis?
opts: A geographic ulcer with a hypopyon
Not the classical simplex description in the deck.
A ring infiltrate in a contact lens wearer
That pattern is associated with other organisms.
A wedge of fibrovascular tissue growing across and over the corneal limbus
That is a pterygium.
A dendritic ulcer with terminal bulbs on fluorescein staining
Correct — the deck's classical description, terminal bulbs included.

set1.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
set1.q: What does the lipid layer of the tear film do?
opts: It prevents evaporation
Correct — the deck's stated function, which is why its loss causes dry eye.
It provides the bulk volume of the tears
That is the aqueous component.
It anchors the tear film to the corneal epithelium
That is the mucin layer's role.
It carries immunoglobulin to the ocular surface
Not the function the deck assigns to lipid.

set1.io: f — Describe the pathogenesis of glaucoma
set1.q: What is the mechanism of primary open-angle glaucoma?
opts: Aqueous production by the ciliary body increases sharply
The deck's mechanism is impaired outflow, not overproduction.
The canal of Schlemm is congenitally absent
Not a mechanism the deck describes.
The iridocorneal angle stays open but microscopic resistance in the trabecular meshwork impairs outflow, raising pressure gradually
Correct — the angle is open; the obstruction is microscopic and downstream.
The iridocorneal angle narrows anatomically and blocks aqueous outflow suddenly
That is angle-closure glaucoma.

set1.io: a — Compare and contrast the neurological anatomy of the eye
set1.q: Which two structures make up the fibrous outer tunic of the eye?
opts: The iris and the lens
The iris is uveal and the lens is not part of a tunic.
The sclera and the cornea
Correct — the protective white coat and the clear refracting window.
The choroid and the ciliary body
Those belong to the uvea, the vascular middle tunic.
The retina and the retinal pigment epithelium
Those form the neurosensory inner tunic.

set1.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
set1.q: How does the deck characterise episcleritis?
opts: A granulomatous blockage of a meibomian gland
That is a chalazion.
A self-limiting inflammatory blush, not vision-threatening and without severe pain
Correct — the deck's characterisation, in deliberate contrast to scleritis.
A vision-threatening emergency with severe deep boring pain and scleral melting
That is scleritis.
An infection of the corneal stroma
That is keratitis.

set1.io: j — Describe visual field deficits according to the area of pathology
set1.q: Which causes does the deck give for an ipsilateral optic nerve lesion?
opts: Temporal lobe surgery
That affects the optic radiation.
Trauma, optic neuritis and ischaemic optic neuropathy
Correct — the deck's three causes at site A.
Pituitary adenoma compression
That is the chiasmal cause.
Posterior cerebral artery occlusion in the occipital lobe
That is the occipital cause.

set1.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
set1.q: What is a hypopyon?
opts: Pus in the anterior chamber
Correct — the deck labels it directly on the image slide.
Blood in the anterior chamber
That is a hyphaema.
Fluid beneath the neurosensory retina
That is a retinal detachment.
Yellow debris beneath the retinal pigment epithelium
Those are drusen.

set1.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
set1.q: What is the fornix, and why does it matter mechanically?
opts: A flexible junctional cul-de-sac that permits free rotation of the globe
Correct — the deck's definition and its mechanical purpose.
The dense fibrous plate giving the eyelid its shape
That is the tarsus.
The sphincteric muscle responsible for blinking
That is orbicularis oculi.
The circular junction where the conjunctiva meets the edge of the cornea
That is the limbus.

set1.io: a — Compare and contrast the neurological anatomy of the eye
set1.q: What makes the eye the only place in the body where live neural tissue can be seen directly?
opts: The retina can be biopsied more safely than any other neural tissue
The deck's point is that no tissue has to be cut at all.
The cornea contains myelinated tracts that can be seen on slit lamp
The cornea's nerves are not what the deck describes here.
The sclera is thin enough to transilluminate the whole globe
Transillumination is not the mechanism the deck gives.
The optic nerve head is visible through the pupil without cutting any tissue
Correct — the deck calls the eye a nervous window for exactly this reason.

set1.io: d — Compare and contrast the conditions caused by abnormal shapes of the eye
set1.q: What is the globe geometry in myopia, and where does the image focus?
opts: The axial globe is too short, so the focal point falls behind the retina
That describes hyperopia.
The globe is normal but the cornea is irregularly curved
That describes astigmatism.
The globe is normal but the lens has lost elasticity
That describes presbyopia.
The axial globe is too long, so the focal point falls in front of the retina
Correct — an elongated globe overshoots, focusing short of the retina.

set1.io: i — Describe the pathologic process of macular degeneration
set1.q: What is the hallmark of dry, atrophic macular degeneration?
opts: Choroidal neovascularisation breaching upward into the subretinal space
That is the wet form.
Neovascularisation on the optic disc
That is proliferative diabetic retinopathy.
Cotton-wool spots in the nerve fibre layer
Those are an ischaemic finding in retinopathy.
Drusen — discrete yellow extracellular debris beneath the pigment epithelium and Bruch membrane
Correct — the deck's hallmark, with its composition and location.

set1.io: j — Describe visual field deficits according to the area of pathology
set1.q: A lesion of the optic tract produces which defect?
opts: Contralateral homonymous hemianopsia
Correct — site C. Past the chiasm, each tract carries the same side of both eyes' fields.
Bitemporal hemianopsia
That is the chiasmal defect.
Monocular blindness
That requires a lesion before the chiasm.
Central scotoma with preserved peripheral vision
That pattern is macular rather than pathway-related.

set1.io: b — Describe the physiological processes of vision
set1.q: Where must light be focused for an image to form?
opts: On the lens itself, which then transmits the signal
The lens refracts light; it does not detect it.
On the retina, after refraction through the cornea and lens
Correct — the deck's description of image formation.
On the choroid, after refraction through the cornea alone
The choroid lies behind the retina and does not receive the focused image.
On the optic disc, where the nerve exits
The optic disc is the blind spot and has no photoreceptors.

set1.io: g — Describe the pathogenesis of cataracts
set1.q: Which medication class does the deck name as a cataract risk?
opts: Chronic antihistamines
Not named by the deck.
Chronic statins
Not named by the deck.
Chronic corticosteroids
Correct — the deck names chronic corticosteroid use.
Chronic beta-blockers
Not a cataract risk in the deck.

set1.io: d — Compare and contrast the conditions caused by abnormal shapes of the eye
set1.q: What can a hyperopic patient see well?
opts: Objects up close
Near vision is the impaired one in hyperopia.
Neither near nor far without correction
Distance vision is preserved.
Only objects directly in the central field
Hyperopia is refractive rather than a field defect.
Objects far away
Correct — hyperopia is farsightedness, so distance vision is the preserved one.

set1.io: i — Describe the pathologic process of macular degeneration
set1.q: What does the deck say about the pathogenesis of macular degeneration overall?
opts: It is unknown
Correct — the deck's slide titles say pathogenesis unknown for both forms.
It is entirely genetic
The deck does not make this claim.
It is entirely driven by ultraviolet exposure
The deck does not attribute it to a single cause.
It is a consequence of raised intraocular pressure
That mechanism belongs to glaucoma.

set1.io: a — Compare and contrast the neurological anatomy of the eye
set1.q: How is the avascular cornea oxygenated?
opts: By the choroidal circulation behind it
The choroid lies at the back of the eye and nourishes the retina.
By direct contact with air and tears
Correct — the deck's stated route for an avascular tissue.
By diffusion from the limbal blood vessels alone
The deck names air and tears rather than limbal supply.
By the aqueous humour circulating through the anterior chamber
Aqueous nourishes the cornea and lens, but the deck names air and tears for oxygen.

set1.io: j — Describe visual field deficits according to the area of pathology
set1.q: Why does a central chiasmal lesion spare nasal vision in both eyes?
opts: Only the crossing nasal retinal fibres are interrupted, and those carry the temporal fields; the temporal retinal fibres travel ipsilaterally and are untouched
Correct — the anatomy of the decussation explains which half is lost.
The lesion damages the temporal retinal fibres instead, and those carry nasal vision
Those fibres do not cross and are not caught by a central lesion.
The macula is spared by a dual blood supply
Macular sparing belongs to occipital lesions.
The lesion affects only one eye at a time
A chiasmal lesion affects both eyes.

set1.io: b — Describe the physiological processes of vision
set1.q: Roughly how many cones are there, and where are they concentrated?
opts: About 6 million, spread evenly across the whole retina
The deck stresses their concentration at the fovea.
About 60 million, concentrated at the optic disc
The optic disc has no photoreceptors at all.
About 6 million, concentrated in the fovea centralis within the macula
Correct — the deck's count and location for cones.
About 120 million, concentrated in the peripheral retina rather than the fovea
That is the rod population and its distribution.

set1.io: e — Compare and contrast the conditions of the eye that are age related
set1.q: Webster tied presbyopia to a letter in an examination mnemonic. Which, and what does it stand for?
opts: The P in PERRLA, for pupils
The P is simply pupils.
The E in PERRLA, for equal
The E is equal.
The A in PERRLA, for accommodation
Correct — pupils equal, round, reactive to light and accommodation. He quizzed the room on it.
The R in PERRLA, for reactive
The R stands for reactive to light, which is not the presbyopia link.

set1.io: h — Compare and contrast the pathogenesis of retinal detachment
set1.q: What symptoms does the deck give for rhegmatogenous detachment?
opts: Severe pain with halos and a fixed mid-dilated pupil
That is acute angle-closure glaucoma.
Slow loss of central detail with progressive distortion of straight lines
That is macular degeneration.
Flashing lights, a shower of floaters, and a curtain falling across the field
Correct — photopsia, floaters, then the curtain.
Gradual painless bilateral blurring with glare at night
That is cataract.

set1.io: i — Describe the pathologic process of macular degeneration
set1.q: Macular degeneration is the leading cause of new-onset blindness in which group?
opts: Children and adolescents
Not a group the deck discusses for this condition.
Adults of any age worldwide
The deck's claim is specific to an age band and country.
Adults over seventy-five in the United States
Correct — the deck's stated epidemiology.
Adults aged twenty to seventy-four in the United States
That is the deck's group for diabetic retinopathy.

set2.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
set2.q: Which lid deformity does the deck associate with dacryoadenitis?
opts: An S-shaped lid deformity
Correct — the deck's characteristic sign for lacrimal gland inflammation.
An inward-turning lid margin
That is entropion.
An outward-turning lid margin
That is ectropion.
A drooping upper lid from levator weakness
That is ptosis.

set2.io: b — Describe the physiological processes of vision
set2.q: Where do impulses travel after leaving the optic nerve?
opts: To the frontal eye fields
Those govern gaze rather than receiving the visual image.
To the superior colliculus alone
The deck's stated destination is the visual cortex.
To the occipital cortex
Correct — the deck routes neural transmission to the occipital cortex.
To the temporal cortex
The temporal lobe carries part of the optic radiation but is not the destination.

set2.io: a — Compare and contrast the neurological anatomy of the eye
set2.q: Which three structures make up the uvea?
opts: The choroid, the retina and the sclera
The retina is the inner tunic and the sclera the outer.
The ciliary body, the lens and the zonules
The lens and zonules are not part of the uvea.
The iris, the cornea and the conjunctiva
The cornea is fibrous and the conjunctiva is a mucosal covering.
The choroid, the ciliary body and the iris
Correct — the vascular middle tunic in full.

set2.io: d — Compare and contrast the conditions caused by abnormal shapes of the eye
set2.q: What can astigmatism combine with, and what happens when it does?
opts: Only presbyopia, and only after the age of forty
Astigmatism is not restricted to combining with presbyopia.
Only glaucoma, through a sustained rise in intraocular pressure over years
There is no such relationship in the deck.
Nothing — it always occurs in isolation
The lecture describes it combining with the other refractive errors.
Myopia or hyperopia, adding a focal-length error to the axis error
Correct — Webster described the two problems stacking.

set2.io: h — Compare and contrast the pathogenesis of retinal detachment
set2.q: Which risk factors does the deck list for rhegmatogenous detachment?
opts: Chronic corticosteroid use, Down syndrome and ultraviolet light exposure
Those are cataract risks.
Posterior vitreous detachment, age, severe myopia, trauma and lattice degeneration
Correct — the deck's five.
Diabetes, prior vitrectomy and retinal trauma surgery
Those are tractional associations.
Sarcoidosis, malignant hypertension and melanoma
Those are exudative causes.

set2.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
set2.q: Which glands are involved in an external as opposed to an internal hordeolum?
opts: External involves a meibomian gland; internal involves the glands of Zeis or Moll
This reverses the deck's assignment.
Both involve the lacrimal gland
The lacrimal gland is not involved in hordeolum.
Both involve the tarsal plate itself rather than any gland
The tarsal plate holds the meibomian glands but is not itself the site.
External involves the glands of Zeis or Moll; internal involves a meibomian gland
Correct — the deck's gland-by-gland distinction.

set2.io: a — Compare and contrast the neurological anatomy of the eye
set2.q: Which three interneuron types modulate the retinal signal before it reaches the ganglion cells?
opts: Bipolar, horizontal and amacrine cells
Correct — the three the deck lists in the neural network.
Bipolar, Müller and astrocyte cells
Müller cells and astrocytes are supporting glia, not the deck's modulating trio.
Horizontal, amacrine and Purkinje cells
Purkinje cells are cerebellar.
Rod, cone and ganglion cells
Those are the input and output, not the interneurons between them.

set2.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
set2.q: What is the mechanism and character of a chalazion?
opts: A cholesterol-filled plaque along the nasal eyelid
That is xanthelasma.
Redundant lid skin with prolapse of orbital fat
That is dermatochalasis.
A chronic, non-tender, sterile granulomatous lipogranuloma of a blocked meibomian gland
Correct — sterile and granulomatous is what separates it from an infection.
An acute, tender, focal abscess of a gland sitting at the eyelid margin
That is a hordeolum.

set2.io: f — Describe the pathogenesis of glaucoma
set2.q: Which symptom set does the deck give for acute angle-closure glaucoma?
opts: Flashing lights, a sudden shower of floaters, and a curtain falling across the field
That is retinal detachment.
Gradual central distortion with a scotoma
That is macular degeneration.
Severe eye pain, headache, halos around lights, cloudy cornea, a fixed mid-dilated pupil, and nausea and vomiting
Correct — the deck's full acute picture.
Painless gradual bilateral blurring with glare at night
That is cataract.

set2.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
set2.q: Diabetic retinopathy is the leading cause of new-onset blindness in which group?
opts: Children under sixteen worldwide
Not the deck's group.
Adults over fifty worldwide
The deck's figure is specific to a narrower band and country.
United States adults aged twenty to seventy-four
Correct — the deck's stated age band.
United States adults aged over seventy-five years
That is the group for macular degeneration.

set2.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
set2.q: What is the natural course of a subconjunctival haemorrhage?
opts: Recurrent by definition, so it requires long-term ophthalmology follow-up
The deck does not describe it this way.
Benign, resolving over one to two weeks with bruise-like colour changes
Correct — the deck's stated course.
Progressive, threatening vision within days
The deck calls it benign.
Permanent, leaving a fibrovascular scar
It resolves.

set2.io: d — Compare and contrast the conditions caused by abnormal shapes of the eye
set2.q: What can a myopic patient see well?
opts: Objects far away
Distance vision is the impaired one in myopia.
Neither near nor far without correction
Near vision is preserved.
Only objects at the extreme periphery
Myopia is a refractive, not a field, problem.
Objects up close
Correct — myopia is nearsightedness, so near vision is the preserved one.

set2.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
set2.q: Which virus does the deck name as the viral cause of conjunctivitis?
opts: Herpes simplex virus
That deck entry is for epithelial keratitis.
Varicella zoster virus
That appears under herpes zoster ophthalmicus.
Cytomegalovirus
Not named by the deck for conjunctivitis.
Adenovirus
Correct — the deck's named viral agent.

set2.io: b — Describe the physiological processes of vision
set2.q: What does aqueous humour nourish?
opts: The optic nerve head
Not a structure the deck says aqueous nourishes.
The extraocular muscles
Those have their own blood supply.
The avascular lens and cornea
Correct — the deck's stated nutritive role for aqueous.
The retina and the choroid
The choroid nourishes the retina; aqueous does not reach them.

set2.io: e — Compare and contrast the conditions of the eye that are age related
set2.q: What is the functional consequence of presbyopia?
opts: Inability to focus on near objects, so reading glasses or bifocals are needed
Correct — the deck's stated consequence, and the everyday presentation.
Inability to focus on distant objects, so distance vision blurs first
Near focus is what is lost.
Loss of peripheral vision
Presbyopia does not affect the visual field.
Loss of colour discrimination
Colour vision is not affected.

set2.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
set2.q: Which patient group does the deck flag as at particular risk in keratitis, and from which organism?
opts: Immunosuppressed patients, from Candida
Not what the deck highlights here.
Contact lens wearers, from Pseudomonas
Correct — the deck names both the group and the organism.
Contact lens wearers, from Staphylococcus aureus
The deck names Pseudomonas for contact lens keratitis.
Elderly patients, from Streptococcus pneumoniae
Not the deck's flagged group or organism.

set2.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
set2.q: What drives the change from non-proliferative to proliferative diabetic retinopathy?
opts: Bacterial collagenase digestion of the retinal surface
That mechanism belongs to corneal ulceration.
Severe ischaemia upregulates vascular endothelial growth factor, producing neovascularisation
Correct — ischaemia to growth factor to new vessels is the deck's step.
Rising intraocular pressure forces new vessels to form
Pressure is not the driver in the deck.
Accumulation of lipofuscin and apolipoprotein beneath the pigment epithelium
That is drusen formation in macular degeneration.

set2.io: i — Describe the pathologic process of macular degeneration
set2.q: What are drusen composed of?
opts: Fibrin and platelet aggregates
Not what the deck describes.
Calcium and phosphate crystals
Not the deck's composition.
Cholesterol esters, as in xanthelasma
That is the lid lesion, with a different composition.
Lipofuscin and apolipoproteins
Correct — the deck's stated composition.

set2.io: j — Describe visual field deficits according to the area of pathology
set2.q: A temporal lobe lesion affecting part of the optic radiation produces which defect?
opts: Monocular blindness
That requires a prechiasmal lesion.
Contralateral superior quadrantanopsia, or pie in the sky
Correct — site D. Webster deferred this one to neurology, but the deck names it.
Contralateral inferior quadrantanopsia instead
The temporal radiation carries the superior field.
Bitemporal hemianopsia
That is a chiasmal lesion.

set2.io: f — Describe the pathogenesis of glaucoma
set2.q: What is iris bombé?
opts: Forward displacement of the iris against the cornea
Correct — the deck uses the term for the forward bowing that closes the angle.
Backward displacement of the iris against the lens
The deck describes forward displacement.
Atrophy of the iris stroma after an acute attack
Not the meaning the deck gives.
Adhesion of the iris to the corneal endothelium
That describes a synechia rather than iris bombé.

set2.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
set2.q: How does panophthalmitis differ from endophthalmitis?
opts: It spares the sclera
It involves all layers, sclera included.
It involves all layers of the globe and may extend into orbital tissue
Correct — the speaker notes draw exactly this distinction.
It involves only the vitreous
That is narrower than endophthalmitis, not broader.
It is limited to the anterior segment and spares the vitreous
The term means the opposite.

set2.io: b — Describe the physiological processes of vision
set2.q: Roughly how many rods are there, and what are they for?
opts: About 120 million, for dim light and peripheral vision
Correct — the deck's count and function for rods.
About 6 million, for dim light and peripheral vision
Six million is the deck's figure for cones.
About 120 million, for colour vision and sharp acuity
Colour and acuity belong to cones.
About 20 million, for colour vision in bright light
Neither the count nor the function matches the deck.

set2.io: g — Describe the pathogenesis of cataracts
set2.q: By what mechanism does diabetes mellitus cause cataract?
opts: Retinal ischaemia releases vascular endothelial growth factor into the lens
That mechanism belongs to proliferative diabetic retinopathy.
Excess glucose is converted to sorbitol, causing osmotic swelling of the lens
Correct — the deck's metabolic mechanism.
Excess glucose glycates the lens capsule until it ruptures
The deck describes osmotic swelling via sorbitol, not capsular rupture.
Hyperglycaemia causes crystallin proteins to aggregate directly
Aggregation is the senile mechanism; diabetes acts through sorbitol.

set2.io: d — Compare and contrast the conditions caused by abnormal shapes of the eye
set2.q: What causes astigmatism?
opts: Irregular corneal or lens curvature creating non-spherical focal points
Correct — the deck's definition, and the reason a single focal point cannot form.
An axial globe that is too long
That is myopia.
An axial globe that is too short
That is hyperopia.
Loss of lens elasticity with age, so the lens can no longer change shape
That is presbyopia.

set2.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
set2.q: Which systemic diseases does the deck link strongly to scleritis?
opts: Rheumatoid arthritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis and systemic vasculitis
Correct — the three the deck names.
Systemic lupus erythematosus, psoriatic arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis
Those are the deck's anterior uveitis associations.
Diabetes mellitus and hypertension
Those drive retinopathy rather than scleritis in this deck.
Sarcoidosis and choroidal melanoma
Those are exudative retinal detachment causes here.

set2.io: d — Compare and contrast the conditions caused by abnormal shapes of the eye
set2.q: What are the two pathophysiological causes of strabismus the deck gives?
opts: Raised intraocular pressure with progressive optic disc cupping and field loss
That is glaucoma.
Lens opacification and loss of the red reflex
That is cataract.
Extraocular muscle imbalance and cranial nerve palsy of the third, fourth or sixth nerves
Correct — the deck's two mechanisms.
Retinal detachment and vitreous haemorrhage
Neither causes misalignment in the deck.

set2.io: g — Describe the pathogenesis of cataracts
set2.q: What is the mechanism of the commonest, senile form of cataract?
opts: Chronic ultraviolet-driven oxidative damage alone
Ultraviolet exposure is listed under environmental causes, not as the senile mechanism.
Progressive insoluble aggregation and deposition of lens crystallin proteins
Correct — the deck's molecular mechanism for the ageing cataract.
Osmotic swelling of the lens driven by sorbitol accumulating inside it
That is the diabetic mechanism, which the deck lists separately.
Rupture of the lens capsule after blunt trauma
That is the traumatic mechanism.

set2.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
set2.q: What single feature separates a pterygium from a pinguecula?
opts: The pterygium encroaches onto the cornea; the pinguecula does not
Correct — Webster put it as crossing the limbus, and called this section important.
The pterygium is yellow; the pinguecula is triangular
The colour and shape descriptions are the wrong way round and are not the separator.
The pterygium is painful; the pinguecula is painless
Pain is not the discriminator the deck gives.
The pterygium is bilateral; the pinguecula is unilateral
Laterality is not the separator.

set2.io: i — Describe the pathologic process of macular degeneration
set2.q: How does dry macular degeneration affect vision?
opts: Rapid central vision loss over days
That is the wet form.
Loss of peripheral vision first, with the central field spared until late
That pattern belongs to open-angle glaucoma.
Sudden painless monocular blindness
That suggests vascular occlusion or optic nerve pathology.
Slow gradual loss of central detail, with distortion and a scotoma
Correct — metamorphopsia and scotoma, developing slowly.

set2.io: e — Compare and contrast the conditions of the eye that are age related
set2.q: What is the mechanism of presbyopia?
opts: The cornea flattens progressively with age, reducing its refractive contribution
The deck attributes it to the lens and ciliary muscle.
The retinal pigment epithelium thins with age
That is relevant to macular degeneration, not presbyopia.
The lens loses elasticity and the ciliary muscle loses accommodation, through sclerosis
Correct — the deck's mechanism, and the point Webster went back to add after saying he was finished.
The axial globe shortens with age
Presbyopia is a lens and ciliary problem, not a globe-shape one.
